title: A Book With Five Doors
subtitle: Who wrote the Lesser Key, and what else is hiding in it
blurb: The Lesser Key turns out to be five books stitched into one, none of them by Solomon, and its first pages are gentler and odder than you were warned.

segments.t: Last night we left a brass jar lying open on a shore in Babylon. Tonight is quieter. Tonight there is a desk, a reading lamp, and a pencil, because they do not let you bring ink into this room.

On the desk is a brown manuscript. The British Library calls it Sloane thirty-eight twenty-five, which is a shelf number, not a title. The handwriting is cramped, seventeenth-century, the ink gone the colour of old tea. It is one of the earliest and most careful copies of the Lesser Key of Solomon that survives. And it raises the awkward question I promised you. If Solomon lived three thousand years ago, and this was copied out in England, in English, who actually wrote it?

Before I answer, turn it over in your hands. In your mind, please. The first surprise is that this is not one book. It is five, stitched together under one name. I think of them as five doors along one corridor. Let me open each of them a crack.

The first door is the one you came for. The Ars Goetia. Ars is only Latin for art. Goetia is Greek, an old word for sorcery, the low and disreputable kind, and it is tied to a word for howling or wailing, the noise of someone crying over a grave. Behind this door are the seventy-two. The book itself describes the room quite cheerfully.

The First Book, or Part, which is a Book concerning Spirits of Evil, and which is termed The Goetia of Solomon, sheweth forth his manner of binding these Spirits for use in things divers. And hereby did he acquire great renown.

The second door opens onto weather. The Ars Theurgia-Goetia. Here are thirty-one chief spirits of the air, emperors and dukes and wandering princes, each one assigned to a point of the compass, like the puffing faces of the winds on an old map. And the book is frank that they are a mixed lot.

The Second Book is one which treateth of Spirits mingled of Good and Evil Natures, the which is entitled The Theurgia-Goetia, or the Magical Wisdom of the Spirits Aerial, whereof some do abide, but certain do wander and abide not.

Some abide, and some wander. Now a documented fact, not a legend. Those names were lifted from a book called the Steganographia, written around fifteen hundred by a German abbot, Johannes Trithemius. It looked like a manual for sending messages by spirit. Much of it turned out to be cryptography, secret writing dressed up as angels. So the second door may open onto a codebook in a costume.

The third door is brighter. The Ars Paulina, the Pauline art, named for the apostle Paul. No demons here. Angels. An angel for each hour of the day and each hour of the night. And an angel for every single degree of the zodiac, three hundred and sixty of them, so that whatever moment you were born, somebody was on duty.

The fourth door is the Ars Almadel, and it is the prettiest room in the house. An almadel is a square tablet of wax, cut with holy names, with a candle standing at each corner. Above it, the book says, appear the angels of four altitudes, four heights of heaven. One is described as coming like a young child dressed in rose-coloured satin, crowned with flowers. I am not making that up. I could not.

And the fifth door is the oldest by far. The Ars Notoria, the notary art. These are medieval prayers, already passing from hand to hand in the twelve hundreds, and what they promise is every student's daydream. Say them rightly, and you receive instant learning. Grammar, logic, a perfect memory, in weeks instead of years. Theologians condemned it, which did wonders for its circulation. And here is a tell. Some copies of the Lesser Key leave this fifth book out entirely.

So. Demons. Spirits of the winds. Angels of the hours. A wax tablet and four candles. Prayers for a perfect memory. Four of the five doors have nothing infernal behind them at all, and those are the four that nobody remembers.

threshold.q: Five doors in one corridor, and tonight you may open only one of them. Which is it?

opts.label: The prayers for memory
opts.reply: The fifth door. Of course. You would trade every demon in the catalogue for one night of remembering everything you ever read. So would most of the monks who copied it. That is the quiet scandal of the Ars Notoria. Its keenest readers were not sorcerers. They were students, with examinations coming.

opts.label: The wax and the candles
opts.reply: The Almadel. You chose the room for its light, and I cannot fault you. Four small flames, warm wax, and a child in rose satin somewhere above the table. It is the gentlest picture in the whole collection. Hardly anyone who buys the book ever reads that far.

opts.label: The demons, still
opts.reply: Honest. So did the printers, and so has nearly every reader since. The first door has the worst reputation and by far the best stories, and it is no accident that it stands at the front. Good. That is the door we will be walking through for ten more nights.

segments.t: Whichever you chose, close it gently. There is still a harder question lying on the desk. Who wrote this? Not Solomon. I will say that plainly, once. There is no ancient scroll, nothing within two and a half thousand years of him. What there is, is a compilation, put together in England around the middle of the sixteen hundreds, by someone we cannot name, out of older pieces. One part of the text even lets slip the year sixteen forty-one, which is careless, for a king who died before Rome was founded.

And you can see the seams. The list of seventy-two comes largely from a catalogue printed in Latin in fifteen seventy-seven by a physician named Johann Weyer, under the wonderful title Pseudomonarchia Daemonum, the false kingdom of demons. It reached our compiler by way of Reginald Scot, who put it into English in fifteen eighty-four. Both were, in their way, debunkers. That story belongs to the tenth night, and it is a good one.

The copies themselves are all late. The one on this desk, Sloane thirty-eight twenty-five. Its neighbour, Sloane twenty-seven thirty-one, which carries the date sixteen eighty-seven and leaves out the fifth book. And Harley sixty-four eighty-three, later still, from the early seventeen hundreds. Then, in nineteen oh four, two English occultists, Samuel Mathers and Aleister Crowley, put it into print. But only the first book. Only the demons.

So why sign it Solomon? For the same reason a cookbook wants a famous chef on the cover. Authority. A spell by nobody is a scribble. A spell by the wisest king who ever lived is a tradition. Scholars call writing that borrows a great name pseudepigrapha. It is the oldest trick in publishing, and I doubt our compiler thought of it as fraud. More as good manners.

One last label to peel off. Why the Lesser Key? Lesser than what? There is another famous grimoire called simply the Key of Solomon, and to keep the two apart, people call that one the Greater Key. It is a different book. Older, born on the continent, and mostly concerned with planetary talismans, the right figure made at the right hour. It has no catalogue of seventy-two. People confuse the two constantly, including people who sell them. Now you will not.

threshold.q: So there is the book with its mask off. Not three thousand years old. Under four hundred, and stitched together from borrowed parts. Tell me honestly. Does that make it less interesting to you, or more?

opts.label: Less. The spell is broken
opts.reply: Fair. A forged signature is a forged signature. But notice that the copyists knew roughly what you know, and kept copying. Whatever held them at the desk, it was not the name on the cover. Stay a little longer and see whether it gets hold of you too. I will not tell anyone.

opts.label: More. Now it is a mystery
opts.reply: I hoped you would say so. A book handed down by a king is only an heirloom. A book assembled in secret, by an unknown English hand, from a doctor's appendix and an abbot's cipher, is a detective story. And we have ten nights left in which to dust it for fingerprints.

opts.label: It never needed to be true
opts.reply: Then you read the way the book wants to be read. Nobody asks whether a ghost story was written by the ghost. The name Solomon is not a claim. It is a candle set in the window, so that you know what kind of house you are walking into.

segments.t: Either way, the pages are the same pages. And last night we stopped after a single name. So let us turn the leaf, and see who the book thought should come directly after Bael. I think they will surprise you.

He is under the Power of the East, and cometh up in the form of an old fair Man, riding upon a Crocodile, carrying a Goshawk upon his fist, and yet mild in appearance. He maketh them to run that stand still, and bringeth back runaways.

Agares. The second spirit, a duke, with thirty-one legions. An old man, fair to look at, riding a crocodile, with a goshawk on his fist. And yet mild in appearance, the book adds, as if it knew how the crocodile would come across. He makes those who stand still run, and he brings runaways back. He teaches every language at once. He pulls down the dignified, churchmen and lords alike. And he causes earthquakes. A kindly grandfather who can shake the ground. His seal is in your grimoire now.

Turn the page. The third spirit is a prince named Vassago, with twenty-six legions, and he has no face. Truly. The book gives him no shape at all. It says only that he is of the same nature as Agares, and then it says this.
This Spirit is of a Good Nature, and his office is to declare things Past and to Come, and to discover all things Hid or Lost.

Of a good nature. In a catalogue of demons. He tells what has been and what will be, and he finds whatever is hidden or lost. And one small honest footnote. Vassago is not in Weyer's printed list at all. He joins the company later, from somewhere nobody has traced. The good-natured one is the one with no known parents.

And the fourth. Change the air for this one. Imagine a shoreline at night. Cold water, no moon. Something small is standing in the shallows, and it is not what you expected to find in a book of devils.
He appeareth in the form of a little Horse or Ass, and then into Human shape doth he change himself at the request of the Master. He speaketh with a hoarse voice.

Samigina. A marquis, with thirty legions. A little horse, or a donkey, who becomes a man if he is asked, and who is hoarse, like Bael. Perhaps it is the damp down there. He teaches all the liberal sciences, the old school subjects, grammar and geometry and the rest. And he gives account of dead souls that died in sin. In the older version that Weyer printed, it is stranger and sadder. There he answers for the souls of those who drowned in the sea. A small rough-voiced horse at the edge of the water, telling you how they are.

Notice what we have just read. An invisible king. A mild old man. A kindly finder of lost things. A talking horse who knows his grammar. Four pages into the most notorious demon book in the English language, and nobody has been torn apart. It gets darker. But the catalogue is gentler and odder than its reputation, and I wanted you to feel that early.

Tomorrow night, the furniture. Because the magician in these pages never simply calls a spirit and hopes. He stands inside one shape, and he makes the spirit stand inside another. The Circle and the Triangle. We will ask what they were for, and what it tells you about a man that he draws a wall around himself before he says hello.

Until then. Three new seals in your grimoire, and five doors in the corridor behind you, four of them still shut. Leave the manuscript on the desk. Pencils only. And if a small horse clears its throat on your way out, be kind. He has had a long night.

glossary.def: The first of the five books of the Lesser Key, and the only one about demons: a catalogue of seventy-two spirits. Goetia is a Greek word for sorcery, linked to a word for howling or wailing.

A book written around 1500 by the German abbot Johannes Trithemius. It reads like spirit magic but much of it conceals a system of secret writing. The second book of the Lesser Key borrows its spirit names.
A square wax tablet inscribed with holy names, with a candle at each corner, described in the fourth book of the Lesser Key as the place where angels of the four altitudes appear.

The notary art: medieval prayers, in circulation by the thirteenth century, that promise rapid learning and a perfect memory. It became the fifth book of the Lesser Key, though some manuscripts omit it.
Writings credited to a famous figure who did not write them. Attaching Solomon's name to a seventeenth-century English compilation is a classic case.
The Key of Solomon, an older and entirely separate grimoire concerned mostly with planetary talismans. The Lesser Key is so called to tell the two apart.
